description:
Could You Feel Two Black Holes Collide?

Episode 58 of a daily journey through the universe. 🌊
Gravitational waves: Einstein predicted them in 1916. On September 14, 2015, LIGO detected ripples from two black holes colliding 1.3 billion light-years away, stretching its 4 km arms by far less than the width of a proton. Nobel Prize 2017.

➡️ Tomorrow, Episode 59: Next stop, how the Sun will die. And what happens to Earth.

Follow so you don't miss a stop. A new episode every day.

#space #gravitationalwaves #astronomy #shorts #science

segments.text: Two black holes collided, a billion light-years away. And we felt it here on Earth.
In nineteen sixteen, Albert Einstein predicted something wild. When heavy objects move, they make ripples in space itself.
segments.headline: Einstein's prediction

segments.text: He thought they'd be so weak that humans could never detect them.
segments.headline: Too weak to detect?

segments.text: Almost a hundred years later, scientists built LIGO: two detectors in the United States with arms four kilometers long, using lasers to measure their length.
segments.headline: LIGO

segments.text: On September fourteenth, twenty fifteen, both detectors felt a tiny wobble.
The ripple changed the length of the four-kilometer arms by far less than the width of a proton.
It came from two black holes, each about thirty times heavier than the Sun, spiraling together and merging.
segments.headline: Two black holes merged

segments.text: That crash happened one point three billion years ago. The ripple had been travelling toward us ever since.
The discovery won the Nobel Prize in Physics in twenty seventeen. Since then, detectors have caught hundreds more.
segments.headline: Nobel Prize, 2017

segments.text: For the first time, we're not just seeing the universe. We're feeling it.
segments.headline: Feeling the universe

segments.text: Tomorrow, the end of our Sun, and what happens to Earth. Next stop: how the Sun will die. Which part surprised you most? Tell me in the comments, and follow for tomorrow's stop.
